summary: Lists short-term requirements for how trusted SIP network nodes pass along a Network Asserted Identity, which is an identity a network intermediary derives after authenticating a user. Unlike a self-chosen alias, it is vouched for by the network. The scope is trusted, securely interconnected networks.

plainLanguage.summary: Anyone can say their name is anything. This document lists what is needed so a trusted phone company can vouch for who someone really is, and pass that on to other trusted companies.

questions: what are the requirements for sip asserted identity
what is a sip trust domain
subtitle: What SIP needs so trusted networks can vouch for who a caller really is, and pass that on only to parties that should hear it.

tldr.problem: SIP lets users assert an identity such as in the From header, but there is no requirement for it to be anything other than the user's desired alias, and user agents often cannot authenticate each other.
tldr.mechanism: A network intermediary derives a Network Asserted Identity after authenticating the user, and shares it only among nodes in a Trust Domain and with nodes that have a secure connection to it and are configured to trust it.
tldr.outcome: The RFC sets short-term requirements for generating, sending, receiving and keeping private such identities; it is not meant for general use between arbitrary Internet hosts.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Trust Domains and directly connected nodes only

today: RFC 3324 is an Informational RFC; the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It states short-term requirements only, for use within trusted, securely interconnected networks.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
SIP lets users assert an identity in several ways, for example in the From: header, but nothing requires it to be more than the user's desired alias. An authenticated identity can be obtained with SIP Digest Authentication or other means, yet user agents do not always have the key information needed to authenticate another one.

A Network Asserted Identity is an identity initially derived by a SIP network intermediary as a result of an authentication process, which may or may not use Digest. This RFC gives short-term requirements for exchanging it inside networks of securely interconnected trusted nodes, and to user agents securely connected to them. General requirements for the Internet at large are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can write any name on a name tag. A trusted front desk that checks your ID and then writes the tag for you is much more believable.

sections.title: Identities and Trust Domains
sections.content:
An identity here is a sip:, sips: or tel: URI, optionally with a Display Name. The URI MUST be meaningful to the domain it names (or the owner of the E.164 number), meaning that used as a Request-URI it would route to the associated user or line. For a Network Asserted Identity, that domain or number owner MUST be within the Trust Domain.

A Trust Domain is a set of SIP nodes trusted to exchange Network Asserted Identity information. A node can be a member only if it is known to comply with a set of specifications called Spec(T). Spec(T) is not a written document; it is an agreed set of information every element knows, covering what is asserted, how it was determined and the privacy policies. Trust Domains are built by people who know their equipment, and simple ones can be joined by bilateral agreements.

Node A is trusted by node B only if there is a secure connection between them and B is configured to say A is in the Trust Domain. B may be outside the domain, for example a UA trusting its home proxy. A secure connection means messages cannot be read or modified undetected by third parties and B can be sure they came from A. The RFC's figure shows that A trusts C but not B, and that E, outside the domain, can trust B without B trusting E.
sections.plainLanguage: A trust domain is a club whose members all follow the same written-down rules. You trust a member only if you have a safe line to them and know they belong to the club.

sections.title: Generating and Moving the Identity
sections.content:
A network intermediary generates the identity after authenticating the user agent. The authentication processes MUST be specified in Spec(T), and a UA shall be able to give a preferred identity that MAY inform what is generated, according to Trust Domain policy.

The transport requirements are:

  • A node shall be able to securely send an identity to, and receive one from, another node it trusts in the domain.
  • A trusted node shall be able to send it to a node outside the domain that trusts it, if the privacy policies of the identified user and the domain allow. This is most often a UA.
  • A node outside the domain shall be able to receive it from a node it trusts, and may treat it as valid for display or as input to services.
  • Information from a node that is not trusted carries no guarantee and MUST NOT be used: not displayed, not passed on, not used as service input.

The identity names the originator of the message carrying it. In an initial INVITE it identifies the caller, in a 180 Ringing response the party who is ringing, and in a 200 response the party who answered. Several identities for one party are allowed if they are of distinct types (sip:, sips:, tel:), and new types shall be addable later.
sections.plainLanguage: The front desk writes the name tag, passes it only to people it trusts, and everyone else must ignore any tag that comes from a stranger.

sections.title: Privacy of the Identity
sections.content:
How privacy requirements are determined is out of scope. It shall be possible to mark a message so its identity is not passed to other users, without saying why. It shall also be possible to indicate that the user asked for this, which implies specific user intent. The mechanism shall support both Trust Domain policies where the two indications are equivalent and ones where they are not.

When the identity is private, a trusted node SHALL NOT send it to a node it does not trust, though it MAY still use it to move the identity within the trusted network. Anonymity requests from users may need additional functionality beyond this, which is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone says "do not tell anyone my name", the front desk keeps the tag inside the club and never hands it to outsiders.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The requirements are NOT intended to give a mechanism with general applicability between arbitrary Internet hosts. They are for a community of devices known to obey Spec(T) and linked by secure connections, and the requirements on security and on deriving the identity initially must be part of Spec(T). They also cover passing the identity over a secure connection to a node outside the domain.

Using the mechanism in any other context has serious security shortcomings: there is absolutely no guarantee that the information has not been modified, or was even correct in the first place. The document has no implications for IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: The name-tag system only works inside a club with safe hallways. Outside, a tag could have been changed on the way, so it proves nothing.

references.text: Rosenberg, J., Schulzrinne, H., Camarillo, G., Johnston, A., Peterson, J., Sparks, R., Handley, M. and E. Schooler, "SIP: Session Initiation Protocol", RFC 3261, June 2002.
